title: Distributed Backpressure & Capacity Triage Runbook
author: Maya Chen
content:
Overview:
This runbook defines the operational play for diagnosing and remediating distributed request-level overloads using backpressure, traffic shaping, and short-term capacity triage. It covers how to: detect when SLOs and error budgets are under pressure, apply automated and manual backpressure controls, scale safely, and ensure graceful degradation while minimizing customer impact.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to: Redwood inference serving tier (proxy/router, model-backend pods, KV cache layer, and GPU serving pool).
- Assumes metrics (Prometheus), tracing (Jaeger), logs (Elastic), and dashboards (Grafana) are available and up-to-date.
- Assumes access to autoscaler (k8s HPA/CustomAutoscaler), traffic router (Traefik/Envoy), and feature flags/traffic-control UI (Operations Console).

Key SLOs & Error Budgets (examples):
| SLO name | Target | Measurement window | Alert trigger | Error budget action |
|----------|--------:|-------------------:|---------------|--------------------|
| API availability (global) | 99.95% | 30d | < 99.9% last 6h | Tier-1 escalation + emergency capacity |
| Generation latency (P95, text-gen) | < 300ms | 7d | P95 > 450ms for 15m | Apply fast-path backpressure, reduce batch sizes |
| Request error rate (5xx) | < 0.5% | 30d | > 1% for 10m | Failover to canary model variants |
| Embeddings throughput (tokens/s) | N/A (throughput SLO) | 7d | Sustained 85% capacity utilization | Scale capacity / enable burst pool |

Monitoring & alerting (what to look for):
- Alerts: availability, elevated 5xx, saturation (cpu/gpu/mem), queue length, request latency spikes, autoscaler errors, prefix-cache hitrate drop.
- Dashboards: "Serving - Global Overview", "Per-model latency & errors", "GPU Utilization & Queues", "Ingress request queues & backpressure signals".

Pre-incident checklist (done by oncall within first 5m):
1) Acknowledge alerts in PagerDuty and mark coordinator.
2) Confirm scope: identify impacted services, regions, and models.
3) Capture baseline: current SLO windows, error-budget burn rate, and traffic trends (last 60m).
4) Check active deploys/rollouts in the last 60 minutes.
5) Verify autoscaler and scheduler health.

Immediate triage steps (0–15 minutes):
1) Identify whether issue is traffic surge vs. infrastructure failure:
   - Traffic surge indicators: sudden increase in ingress rate, client-side burst patterns, queue growth across replicas.
   - Infra failure indicators: nodes lost, OOM/killed pods, kernel-level errors, increased 5xx with unchanged ingress.
2) If infra failure, follow the standard node/pod remediation runbook and notify SRE infra leads.
3) If traffic surge or mixed: apply backpressure and traffic shaping (see Backpressure Controls).
4) Throttle non-critical routes: use rate-limit rules at the router for least-critical routes (e.g., batched bulk clients, non-real-time pipelines).
5) Shift traffic to lower-cost-safe models or smaller sequence-length variants when possible (model-fallback).

Backpressure controls (ordered by speed/safety):
| Control | Scope | Typical effect | When to use |
|---------|-------|---------------|-------------|
| Router-level rate limits | Ingress route | Immediate drop/429 to clients | Large external client floods |
| Client-side Retry-Control header | Specific client token | Reduces retries, buys time | Misbehaving SDKs or aggressive retries |
| Prefix / KV cache warm-up | Model backends | Reduce repeated compute for hot prefixes | Sudden repeated prompts causing recompute |
| Per-model concurrency cap | Backend pods | Limits active decodes per GPU | Protects GPU memory/throughput under overload |
| Queue depth signal to autoscaler | Internal | Triggers faster scale up | When autoscaler lagging behind demand |

Applying backpressure (runbook actions):
1) Router rate-limit: add a temporary rate-limit rule with a 5–15 minute TTL for the offending route. Example Envoy command (Ops Console):
   - Set: limit-by:origin, requests_per_minute: 1000 (adjust per route)
2) Set per-model concurrency cap via the Control Plane API:
   - curl -X POST https://control-plane.internal/api/v1/models/{model}/concurrency -d '{"max_concurrency": 4}'
3) Toggle client retry-control header override for known SDK versions via feature flag: ops/featureflags:set retry_control_override=true
4) If clients are internal, contact integration owners to reduce client-side concurrency immediately.

Capacity triage and safe scaling:
- Goal: scale quickly enough to stop SLO burn without overshooting and causing instability/queue storms.
1) Check current autoscaler state and pending scaling events: kubectl get hpa && describe hpa {serving-hpa}.
2) If autoscaler is stuck (OOMKilled pods, insufficient nodes), scale cluster capacity (add nodes) via cloud autoscaling group or request temporary burst pool (Dedicated burst).
3) If safe: perform a manual, staged scale-up of serving replicas by +25% steps with 2–4 minute stabilization windows, validating latency and queue depth after each step.
4) If GPU node provisioning latency is high (> 10m), enable temporary CPU-based fallbacks for small models or use lower-precision quantized variants as an intermediate mitigation.

Traffic shaping and routing strategies:
- Prefer weighted routing to fallback models over hard-blocking when possible to preserve degraded functionality.
- Use canary circuit-breakers for new routes. Example Grafana/Alert procedure: create evaluation rule to automatically shift 10% traffic away if P95 > threshold for 10m.

Safe rollback and failover considerations:
- If a recent rollout correlates with the onset, immediately pause/cancel the rollout and rollback if errors continue.
- Do not perform large config rollbacks while the system is under autoscaling churn unless they are the confirmed cause.

Communications and escalation (first 30m):
1) Post incident status to #incidents and the customer status page if public impact is expected.
2) Notify product/support owners for customers in the affected cohort.
3) If error budget breach is likely, page SRE manager and the product SLO owner.

Post-incident tasks and incident review template (owners and deadlines):
- Short incident summary (by oncall) — due within 24h.
- Timeline & evidence (traces, graphs, commands executed) — due within 48h.
- Root cause hypothesis and corrective actions — 72h.
- Action item owners + due dates — tracked in JIRA; follow-up review in next SRE weekly.

Incident review checklist (to include in postmortem):
1) Was backpressure applied? What controls and when?
2) Did capacity autoscaling respond? Times and deltas.
3) Were model fallbacks or quantized variants used? Effectiveness measured.
4) Customer impact classification and whether SLOs were missed.
5) Recommendations to prevent recurrence (tooling, thresholds, playbook updates).

Operational tooling & queries (quick references):
- Prometheus: current ingress rate (total_requests per 10s), P95 latency: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le)).
- Check GPU queue depth: sum(serving_pending_tasks) by (node,model).
- Identify hot prefixes: topk(20, sum(rate(reqs_total[5m])) by (prompt_hash)).
- Example kubectl checks:
  - kubectl get pods -n redwood-serving -o wide
  - kubectl describe hpa serving-backend

Ownership and runbook maintenance:
- Runbook owner: Maya Chen (SRE – Serving).
- Review cadence: quarterly, or after any incident that used this runbook. Update the runbook within 7 days after each major incident.

Appendix: sample incident timeline entry (format):
- 2026-02-09T14:03Z — Alert: P95 text-gen latency > 450ms (15m).
- 14:07 — Router rate-limit applied to /v1/generate for API key X (5m TTL).
- 14:12 — Per-model concurrency cap set to 6 for model-abc.
- 14:20 — Manual scale-up +25% (3 -> 4 replicas). P95 reduced to 320ms.
- 15:40 — Autoscaler caught up; rollback rate-limit at 15:45.
